opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'd say we're still early. Compared to vision or hearing, digital olfaction is decades behind. For vision we have cameras, for sound we have microphones, and both are cheap, small, and very good, often better than our own senses in some respects. There's no equivalent for smell yet. There's no device you can buy that does what your nose does, broadly and reliably.

What exists today falls into a few buckets. There are analytical instruments like gas chromatography–mass spectrometry. They're incredibly precise and can tell you which molecules are in a sample and at what concentrations. But they're big, expensive, slow, and they need trained operators. They tell you the chemistry, not the smell. Knowing what's in the vial doesn't tell you how a person would perceive it.

Then there's the family of "electronic noses": arrays of chemical sensors like metal-oxide sensors, conducting polymers, and so on. They've been around since the eighties and they're useful for narrow tasks, like detecting one specific gas or flagging spoilage in a controlled setting. But they drift, they're sensitive to humidity and temperature, and they generalize poorly. They're nowhere near the breadth of a biological nose, which has around 400 types of olfactory receptors and can pick up some compounds at parts per trillion.

And then there's a newer and more exciting direction: using biology itself, meaning olfactory receptors expressed in cells or put onto chips, paired with machine learning. I'm optimistic about that because nature has already solved the sensing problem, and we may be able to borrow the hardware.

But I'd argue the hardware isn't the only bottleneck. A huge missing piece has been the map: a principled way to go from a molecule's structure to what it smells like. Vision had color space. We understood red, green, and blue, and how wavelengths map to perception. Olfaction never had that. So a lot of our work has been on that side, using machine learning, especially graph neural networks, to predict odor from molecular structure. We built what we call a principal odor map, and it can predict how a molecule will smell about as well as a trained human panelist.

So my overall assessment is that the sensing side is improving but still immature, and the representation side is making real progress now. When those two come together, cheap and broad sensors plus a good map from chemistry to perception, I think you'll see computers that can genuinely smell. We aren't there yet, but for the first time it feels like the path is visible.

r001.rationale: The response describes some sensing instruments as big, expensive, slow, and operator-dependent, but it does not compare their state to the mainframe era of computing.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. So the honest answer is that we're very early, and I think it helps to put it in historical perspective. If you think about how computers got vision and hearing, the sensors came first. Cameras and microphones existed for about a century before deep learning made it possible to actually understand what was coming through them. Smell is in a different situation. There is no equivalent of a camera for odor. There's no cheap, ubiquitous, reliable sensor that you can buy off the shelf and that gives you a faithful representation of what's in the air.

What does exist falls into a few buckets. On one end you have analytical chemistry instruments, things like gas chromatography and mass spectrometry. Those are incredibly precise, they can tell you which molecules are present and in roughly what quantities, but they're the size of a refrigerator, they cost hundreds of thousands of dollars, and a single measurement can take an hour. So they're wonderful for research, but they're not going to end up in your phone.

On the other end you have what people have called electronic noses for about thirty years now, which are typically arrays of metal oxide sensors or polymer sensors that change resistance when molecules land on them. The problem is that they drift over time, they're sensitive to humidity and temperature, and two sensors that are nominally identical will give you different readings. So the data you collect this week doesn't necessarily mean the same thing next week, and that's a nightmare for machine learning. A lot of the field has been stuck there, where you can get a demo working in a lab but it doesn't generalize.

What I find exciting is that the two halves of the problem are starting to come together. On the software side, we now have models that can predict what a molecule smells like from its structure with roughly the accuracy of a trained human panelist, and that gives you a kind of map, an odor space, that you can embed sensor readings into. On the hardware side, there's real progress in things like printed sensor arrays, bio-inspired sensors that use actual olfactory receptor proteins, and simply having many more sensor channels so that you can be robust to any individual one misbehaving. The analogy I like is that a single pixel is useless, but a million slightly noisy pixels plus a good model gets you a camera.

So if you asked me to grade it, I'd say the understanding side has moved from near zero to genuinely useful in the last five or six years, and the sensing side is maybe where digital cameras were in the early eighties. The pieces exist, they're clunky and expensive, and the thing that will change the trajectory is a sensor that is cheap enough and stable enough that you can collect data at scale. Once that happens, I think progress will be very fast, because all the machine learning infrastructure is already waiting for it.

r001.rationale: The response describes lab instruments as large and expensive and compares the sensing side to early-1980s digital cameras, but it does not compare current chemical-sensing devices to the mainframe era of computing.

astra-6.text:
I think we’re still very early. We have cameras that give computers vision and microphones that give them hearing, but we don’t have an equivalent for smell that’s inexpensive, robust, and general purpose.

There are devices that detect particular chemicals, and there are sophisticated instruments that can tell you a lot about what’s in a sample. But detecting a chemical and understanding what something smells like are different problems. A measurement of the molecules in the air doesn’t automatically tell you how a person would perceive that mixture.

So there are two pieces that need to come together: the hardware to capture useful information about the chemical world, and the models to interpret it. We’ve made progress on both, but I wouldn’t say we have the olfactory equivalent of a camera yet.

r001.rationale: The response describes chemical-sensing devices as limited and sophisticated instruments as available, but it does not compare their laboratory-bound state to the mainframe era of computing.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’re still pretty early. We have devices that can detect particular chemicals very well, but that’s different from giving a computer a general sense of smell. You can build a sensor for a specific gas, for example, without being able to tell whether something smells like coffee or a rose.

The hard part is getting a rich, reliable signal across the enormous variety of molecules out there—and then interpreting that signal. Sensors can drift, humidity can affect them, and real-world smells are mixtures. So the question isn’t just, “Can I detect something?” It’s, “Can I recognize it consistently, in a new environment, and relate that measurement to what a person would smell?”

I’m optimistic, but I don’t think we have the equivalent of a camera or a microphone for smell yet. There’s still important work to do on both the hardware and the computational side.

r001.rationale: The response says smell-sensing devices are still early and describes their limitations, but it does not characterize them as laboratory-bound or compare their state to the mainframe era of computing.
